children: Britain sold £900 million ($1.21 billion) of inflation-linked debt on Thursday at the highest real yield in 25 years, highlighting the growing cost of issuing long-dated government debt.

The 1.875% 2049 index-linked gilt (GBIL0F49=), which was first launched in July last year, sold at auction at a real yield of 2.496% - the highest real yield since the auction of a 10-year index-linked gilt in April 2001.

The real yield represents the yield on top of the retail price index measure of inflation that is paid on British index-linked government debt and reflects how much compensation – on top of protection against inflation – investors require to hold British debt rather than other assets.

The relatively modest £900 million sale attracted 3.22 billion pounds in bids, giving a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.58, the highest in Debt Management Office records of index-linked gilt auctions dating back to 1998.

On Wednesday, benchmark 20-year gilt yields (GB20YT=RR) rose to their highest since 1998, driven by a global rise in the cost of borrowing due to inflation pressure caused by the Iran war as well as concerns about Britain's high government borrowing.
